newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Third World body says "corporate greed" wins in WTO.
newsitem.headline: Third World body says "corporate greed" wins in WTO.

text.p: Third World development groups said on Thursday "corporate greed" was winning out at the World Trade Organisation's ministerial conference, leaving poor people round the globe to suffer.

United in the Malaysia-based Third World Network (TWN), they also condemned the "secretive and undemocratic nature" of the week-long gathering, arguing many developing countries had been excluded from vital negotiations.

"It is likely that the rich countries will get their way...once again ignoring the needs and problems of the South," a statement from the TWN declared. The interests of the poorer countries had been "brushed aside."

"In the end, the real winners of the ministerial conference will be corporate greed, whilst the interests of the people, especially in developing countries, will be sold out further," the statement said.
The TWN links non-governmental organisations (NGOs) in Asia, Latin America and Africa.

The statement echoed complaints voiced by many delegates from both richer emerging economies and the world's 49 least-developed countries or LDCs at the conference that their central concerns had been largely ignored.

"Everyone in the WTO agreed before we came here that the most important thing to discuss was implementation of the Uruguay Round accords," said a senior trade diplomat from one of the major Asian states.
"But where have we actually been talking seriously about this in Singapore? Nowhere."

The Uruguay Round of global trade negotiations from 1986-93 shaped a wide-ranging package of accords on slashing tariffs and bringing service industries, farm produce and textiles, as well as intellectual property rights under firm trade rules.

Developing countries argue that this had involved them in complicated programmes of altering domestic laws for which they were ill-prepared, as well as commitments which they barely understood and now found working against their interests.

Under "implementation", nearly all of these states were seeking discussion in Singapore on easing their overall obligations, and the LDCs -- many of whom see their food bills soaring -- wanted a special accord to alleviate their plight.
"Instead, the Ministerial has been hijacked by Infotec and by the new issues that the big powers want to force onto us, which will only make our problems worse," said one Asian LDC negotiatior.

"Infotec" refers to the deal on removing all tariffs on most information technology products by the year 2000 carved out by the United States and the European Union with Canadian and Japanese backing in Singapore.

The "new issues" are investment, competition and government procurement policies -- on which the big four now have language close to their own wishes in a final ministerial Declaration -- and labour conditions, on which the battle continues.

The TWN statement said the process adopted at the meeting, the 128-nation WTO's first at minister level, was shaped to make it easier for the major countries "to 'persuade', pressurise and coerce the developing countries to agree to their agenda.
When it was finished, the Declaration would be thrown to developing countries who had been left outside a smaller caucus "to accept and sign on," the TWN said.
